title: Is Anything Too Hard for Yahweh? — Three Men, a Laugh, Intercession
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. The last lesson left us with a ninety-nine-year-old man who laughed in the morning, took up a knife in the afternoon, and on that very day finished everything God had told him to do.
Today, in this chapter, God comes in person to the door of his tent. And somewhere in this chapter, one person's laugh gets overheard.

So let me put a question to you first. Is there something you have stopped being able to laugh about? Not anger, not grief — the kind of laugh that comes after you have waited too long and shut the door yourself. Somebody brings it up again, and you give a small smile, and inside you think: never mind, let it go.
Let me put the answer up front. That silent laugh inside you — he heard it, and he did not withdraw the promise because of it. A year later, that bitter laugh was rewritten into the name of a child.
Verse 1: "Yahweh appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day."
Brothers and sisters — "in the heat of the day." That is the hour of the day when nobody wants to move. And remember, he had been circumcised only days before, and he was ninety-nine years old.
Then verse 2: "He lifted up his eyes and looked, and saw that three men stood near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself to the earth."
He ran. וַיָּרָץ (*vayarats*). A ninety-nine-year-old man, freshly under the knife, dozing through the hottest hour of the noon — he sees three strangers, and he runs.

In the verses that follow, the writer piles up one quick verb after another. Verse 6: "Abraham hurried into the tent to Sarah, and said, 'Quickly prepare three seahs of fine meal, knead it, and make cakes.'" Verse 7: "Abraham ran to the herd … and gave it to the servant. He hurried to dress it."
Hurried, quickly, ran, hurried. In the space of a few short verses the page is full of words like that.

And notice how modest the words coming out of his mouth are: "please don't go away from your servant. Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet … I will get a piece of bread so you can refresh your heart." A little water. A piece of bread.

And then what does he actually do? Three seahs of fine meal — that is something over twenty kilograms of flour, enough bread for dozens of people. A tender and good calf. Butter and milk. He speaks small, and he acts large.

Brothers and sisters, this passage is the Bible's model of hospitality. And Hebrews 13:2 says, "Don't forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it." That sentence is talking about this chapter.

Verse 8 has an even lovelier detail: "He stood by them under the tree, and they ate." He did not sit down and eat with them; he stood at the side and waited on them. One of the wealthiest men of his day, standing to serve three travel-stained strangers.
Who exactly were those three men? Was one of them Yahweh?

The text is written with great delicacy. Verse 1 says, "Yahweh appeared to him", and then it says he saw "three men". Verse 22 says the two went off towards Sodom, "but Abraham stood yet before Yahweh." And the opening of chapter 19 says, "The two angels came to Sodom at evening." So the text itself points this out: one of them speaks in the person of Yahweh, and the other two are angels. Down the centuries interpreters have read that one as an appearance of Christ before the incarnation. That is a respectable traditional reading, but you must say plainly that it is an inference. The safe way to preach it is this: Scripture states outright that one of them is Yahweh, and the remaining details do not need to be filled in on Scripture's behalf.
Abraham ran to receive his guests. What is there to preach in that?

In that culture an elderly patriarch did not run; running cost a man his standing. Yet verse 2 says that "when he saw them, he ran to meet them from the tent door"; verse 6 says he "hurried into the tent to Sarah"; verse 7 says he "ran to the herd". Three hurried movements, written one straight after another. And what he says out loud is "a piece of bread", while what he actually produces is three seahs of fine meal and a tender and good calf — banquet proportions. The reminder for us is this: real hospitality says little and does much. Hebrews 13 says, "Don't forget to show hospitality to strangers, for in doing so, some have entertained angels without knowing it", and that is precisely this passage.
2. A Light from the Original: the Laugh That Made No Sound
Verse 9: "They asked him, 'Where is Sarah, your wife?'"
Brothers and sisters, there is a clue hidden in that sentence. The name "Sarah" was given only in the previous chapter. These visitors knew her new name.
Verse 10: "He said, 'I will certainly return to you at about this time next year; and behold, Sarah your wife will have a son.' Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him."
"At about this time next year" is כָּעֵת חַיָּה (*ka'et chayah*), literally "according to the living time" — it means the full cycle of a pregnancy carried to term. God gave a very concrete date.

Verse 11: "Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing." The Hebrew behind "well advanced in age" is בָּאִים בַּיָּמִים (*ba'im bayamim*), literally "come into the days" — not merely old, but far along the road. And the text adds, without flinching from it, a plain physiological fact: the possibility had already dropped to zero.
Verse 12: "Sarah laughed within herself, saying, 'After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?'"
"Laughed within herself" — she made no sound. This was a laugh inside a tent, with her back turned, seen by nobody, a laugh that stirred only on the inside of her.
Then verse 13: "Yahweh said to Abraham, 'Why did Sarah laugh …'"
Brothers and sisters, stop here for a moment. She laughed on the inside — and he heard it.

This can be a terrifying thing, and it can be the greatest comfort in the world, and which of the two it is depends entirely on who God is in your heart. If he is a God hunting for faults, then "even the inside of you is overheard" is a horror. If he is a God searching for you, then "even the inside of you is overheard" is the greatest comfort there is — because it means you do not have to tidy yourself up first. He already knows.

And verse 14 is the centre of the whole chapter: "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" The Hebrew behind "too hard" is הֲיִפָּלֵא (*hayipale*), from a root meaning "wonderful, too difficult, beyond the ordinary".

Brothers and sisters, notice that this sentence is not a slogan to be hung on a wall. It is spoken to the body of an eighty-nine-year-old woman. Say "God can do anything" often enough and it turns into a polite formula; this verse forces you to put it into the singular — in that impossible thing of mine, is it too hard for him?
Verse 15 gives a very honest ending: "Then Sarah denied it, saying, 'I didn't laugh,' for she was afraid. He said, 'No, but you did laugh.'"

Brothers and sisters, what God pressed on was not the laugh. It was the sentence "I didn't laugh." He has room for your laughter; he has no room for you saying "I didn't laugh." And notice that none of this bought her any punishment — in the chapter that follows she conceives all the same, and in chapter 21 the child is born all the same.
Sarah laughed inside herself and God heard it. Does that mean God is collecting evidence against people?

Look first at how God handled it. He did not shame her in front of everybody. He asked Abraham, "Why did Sarah laugh?", and then said the sentence at the heart of the chapter: "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" Sarah was afraid and denied it, and all God answered was, "No, but you did laugh" — he set the truth down plainly and did not press any further. So what this passage gives us is not "God is watching you", but "God knows even what you have not said out loud, and he still intends to do the thing he promised." In practice that means you do not have to put on a performance in his presence. Those doubts inside you that you dare not speak — he has known them all along, and his promise is not cancelled by them.
Is Sarah's laugh connected to the name Isaac later on?

It is, and it is one of the tenderest arrangements in the whole book. "Isaac" (יִצְחָק, *Yitzchak*) simply means "he laughs". In chapter 17 Abraham laughed first; in chapter 18 Sarah laughed; and in chapter 21, when the child was born, Sarah said, "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me." The same word — turned from the laugh of unbelief into the laugh of joy. God did not take the laugh away; he changed what was inside it. That is an enormous comfort for us: the thing you smile at bitterly or coldly today may be the very thing God uses one day to make you laugh for real. And that child's name would go on reminding the whole household — they had once laughed, and God did it anyway.
3. Will I Hide from Abraham What I Do?
In verse 16 the three visitors rise and look out towards Sodom, and Abraham walks along with them to see them on their way.
Then in verse 17 God says something most unusual: "Yahweh said, 'Will I hide from Abraham what I do?'"
Brothers and sisters, that is one of the most moving sentences in the whole Bible. God is talking to himself, and the content of it is this: shall I tell him about this?
And verse 19 gives the reason: "For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice."

God tells his plan to a man who will pass it on. Brothers and sisters, this is how God chooses people. He is not looking for the most capable one; he is looking for the one who will teach this to the generation coming after him.

Verses 20 and 21: "Yahweh said, 'Because the cry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and because their sin is very grievous, I will go down now, and see whether their deeds are as bad as the reports which have come to me. If not, I will know.'"
"I will go down now, and see" — you heard the same grammar in Genesis 11:5. This is courtroom language: before any verdict, an inspection in person. God never decides a case on hearsay.

Brothers and sisters, this verse is worth committing to memory for every one of us who forwards messages. If even God "goes down to see", what gives us the right to read one forwarded post and pronounce a person guilty?
God says, "Will I hide from Abraham what I do?" Why would God tell a human being what he is about to do?

Genesis 18:17–19 gives the reason: "For I have known him, to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh." That is to say, God let him know because he wanted him to teach the generations after him. This matters a great deal. Revelation given to a person is never given to satisfy curiosity; it is given so that the person will carry responsibility. And that is intensely practical for us: if the truth you know has not got into how you raise your children, how you treat people and how you make decisions, then that knowing has been wasted. Notice too that God here treats Abraham as a conversation partner the way a friend does — and that is the highest picture of prayer there is. Not asking a favour, but working alongside.
4. Fifty Down to Ten: the Boldness of Intercession
Verse 22: "The men turned from there, and went toward Sodom, but Abraham stood yet before Yahweh."
What follows is the most famous act of intercession in the Bible. He begins by asking about fifty righteous men, and comes down step by step — forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten.
Brothers and sisters, I want you to notice three things.

First, who spoke first. Verse 17 says, "Will I hide from Abraham what I do?" — it was God who drew him in. So this conversation is not a man refusing to let go of God. It is God putting what is on his heart into words first, and then waiting for the man to open his mouth. God is teaching him how to intercede.

Second, his posture. Verse 27: "See now, I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes." Verse 30: "Oh don't let the Lord be angry, and I will speak." Brothers and sisters, he is bold and he knows exactly who he is, and both of those are true at the same moment. That is what real intercession looks like — knowing I am dust and ashes, knowing he is the Judge of all the earth, and opening my mouth anyway.

Third, who he is praying for. Sodom is a city that has nothing to do with him, and an unrighteous city at that — the city where the nephew who once picked out the best piece of land for himself is now living. He is pleading for a crowd of people who, as we would say, had it coming.
Brothers and sisters, the hardest step in intercession is not speaking up for the people you love. It is speaking up for the people you think had it coming. Is there a Sodom on your prayer list?
And the conversation stops at ten. He asked his way down to ten and then stopped, and God went his way. There were not even ten in that city.
But turn over to Genesis 19:29: "When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot lived."
Brothers and sisters, he asked for a city, and God saved a man. What he asked for did not come about — and what God did was more precise than what he had asked.
Going from fifty down to ten — was Abraham haggling with God?

His own words are deeply humble: "I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes"; "Oh don't let the Lord be angry." So this is not haggling. It is a man, inside the space God had given him, testing step by step how wide God's mercy runs. And here is what deserves attention: every single time, God said yes. The one who stopped was Abraham, not God. That is very instructive for our own intercession — we usually stop far too early. We must also be honest: in the end Sodom was still destroyed, and there were not even ten righteous men in it. So intercession does not guarantee an outcome. But chapter 19 says, "God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out of the middle of the overthrow" — that act of intercession saved a man.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" as a guarantee that whatever you ask for you will get. That sentence speaks about God's power; it is not a warranty that every wish will be granted. The same God — Paul begged him three times to take the thorn away, and he said, "My grace is sufficient for you." If you preach this sentence as a formula, then when something does not come about, the congregation will conclude that their own faith was not strong enough — and that is a very deep injury to inflict on people.

The second is treating Sarah's laugh as a cautionary tale to scold people with. God did point it out — but he did not withdraw the promise, and later he turned that very laugh into the child's name. More importantly, Hebrews 11:11 puts Sarah on the roll of faith. If all you do with her is take her laugh and lecture people with it, you have missed the whole stretch of grace that surrounds it.

The third is preaching intercession as a negotiating technique for changing God's mind. Abraham's posture is, "I have taken it on myself to speak to the Lord, although I am dust and ashes." If you preach it as a skill — start at fifty and bargain your way down — you have turned prayer into haggling over a price. What the congregation ought to learn here is boldness inside reverence, not a method to operate.

The fourth is preaching the judgement on Sodom as propaganda for a single charge. Ezekiel 16:49 lists Sodom's sin: "pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease was in her and in her daughters. She also didn't strengthen the hand of the poor and needy." And Jude 7 speaks of their going after strange flesh. Scripture's indictment has several layers; not one of them needs to be deleted, and not one of them may be added to. Pick out a single item and preach only that, and the pulpit becomes a weapon aimed at one particular group of people.

The fifth is speaking about the identity of the three visitors with more certainty than the text does. Verse 1 says that Yahweh appeared, and Genesis 19:1 says, "The two angels came to Sodom at evening" — so one of them is Yahweh, and the other two are angels. Some read the three as an appearance of the Trinity; the text does not say that. When you preach, you do not need to turn an inference into a settled conclusion for the sake of effect.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese people take hospitality extremely seriously, but our hospitality often carries face along with it — the dishes must be many, the cups must be full, nobody may be allowed to think us stingy. Is Abraham's welcome the same thing? Brothers and sisters, part of it is very much alike, and one thing is decisively different. What is alike is the generosity: three seahs of fine meal, a tender and good calf, far beyond anything that was needed. What is different is in verse 8: "He stood by them under the tree." Our hospitality usually has the host sitting in the place of honour, being thanked and being praised; he stood at the side and served. And what came out of his mouth was "a little water, a piece of bread" — he made the occasion large and made himself small. Chinese display usually runs the other way round: make the occasion large, and make yourself large as well. So the lesson this passage gives us is not "be more generous." It is "after you have been generous, do not go and sit in the place of honour."

The second question: an elder in my family is seriously ill, or something has dragged on for a very long time — should I keep on asking? Does it look like a lack of faith, like pestering God? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives an extremely clear answer: God himself taught Abraham how to pester him. God is the one who says, "Will I hide from Abraham what I do?", and then stops and waits for the man to open his mouth, and lets him go all the way from fifty down to ten. Not once does God say, "Why are you still asking?" And in Luke 18, in the parable of the unrighteous judge and the widow, the reason the Lord Jesus told that parable — the text says it outright — is "that they must always pray and not give up." So please keep asking. But let me add two pastoral sentences. First, the posture of intercession has to be right: carry the reverence of "although I am dust and ashes", not the resentment of "you owe me an explanation." Second, watch for God answering in a way you never thought of — Abraham asked for a city, and God saved a man. So while you are asking, leave a space open for God's other kind of answer.
Does interceding for other people actually do anything? Hasn't God already decided?

Scripture teaches two things at once: God has his own plan, and God really does answer prayer. How those two stand together is a long-running theological discussion, and we do not have to announce from the pulpit that we have solved it. What is certain is Scripture's own attitude. James says, "The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective." The Lord Jesus prayed through the night. Paul asked again and again for people to intercede for him. So rather than tangling ourselves up in the mechanism, we had far better simply do it. And chapter 18 offers a very practical hint: intercession changes the intercessor first. From the moment Abraham prayed for Sodom, his relationship with that city was no longer the same. It is very hard to go on looking down on somebody you are praying for.
7. Living 321 Out — Knowing Who I Am and Knowing Who He Is
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Abraham stood and waited on three guests. And in John 13, at the last supper, the Lord Jesus rose from the table, took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel round himself, and knelt down to wash his disciples' feet. Brothers and sisters, here is my role model: at the most honoured moment of his life, he chose to stand at the side and serve. The true stature of a person is measured by where he stands at the very moment he is most entitled to sit in the place of honour.

The Bible is my standard — one of the standards this chapter hands us is in verse 19. God chose him "to the end that he may command his children and his household after him, that they may keep the way of Yahweh, to do righteousness and justice." Which is to say: a standard is meant to be handed on. A standard you apply only to yourself and never teach to the next generation stops with you.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice how God began that act of intercession. He put what was on his heart into words first, and then he waited. Brothers and sisters, very often a burden for a person or a situation comes over us out of nowhere, and it is not something we thought up ourselves; it is that he told us what was on his heart first. Romans 8:26 says that the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.

Let Jesus be King — "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" That is handing the boundary of what is possible back to God. Brothers and sisters, we habitually fix God's range for him before we have even begun to pray — this thing is probably impossible, that thing I would be embarrassed to ask for. Letting Jesus be King means no longer using my own experience to limit what he is able to do.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — the answer in verse 14 is not "you need more faith", it is "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" The focus moves off human capacity and onto God's power. And after Isaac was born, what Sarah said was, "God has made me laugh" — she made it perfectly clear who the glory belonged to.

Establish God's system — "Will I hide from Abraham what I do?", because he will command his children after him. Brothers and sisters, God's system has succession built into it. So to establish God's system is to hand what is on God's heart over to the next generation — not merely to hand down the rules, but to hand down the things God cares about. Do your children know what you weep over? Do they know who you pray for?

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We often say, "the focus is on Jesus, not on myself", and that is right. But this chapter shows us a balance. When Abraham interceded, he said, very plainly, "although I am dust and ashes" — he knew exactly who he was. So keeping the focus off myself is not the same thing as forgetting who I am. A healthy spiritual life holds two things at the same time: I know I am dust and ashes, so I am never arrogant; I know he invited me, so I dare to open my mouth. Take only the first half and you end up not daring to pray at all. Take only the second half and you end up treating God as a wish-granting machine.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Laugh
Brothers and sisters, the same soundless laugh, falling into four kinds of heart, sounds like four completely different things.

The proud heart says, "Sarah's faith was really poor." What this heart most wants to do when the reading is over is to comment on that laugh. Brothers and sisters, go back and read Genesis 17:17 — Abraham laughed too, and he laughed lying face down on the ground. The text writes down both of their laughs. If the only one you remember to scold is one of the two, that is usually not exegesis; that is favouritism.

The fearful heart says, "He hears even what I think on the inside." This heart trembles at the thought that God knows every one of its notions. To a heart like that I want to say: look at what he did after he knew. He did not withdraw the promise. He did not punish her. He did not replace her with somebody else. All he said was, "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" He heard the doubt inside you, and what he answered with was his own power, not your failure.

The ashamed heart says, "I stopped daring to ask a long time ago." You may have asked for many years and then one day simply stopped mentioning it, because every time you mention it you have to hurt all over again. Brothers and sisters, Sarah's laugh is exactly that sort of laugh — it is not contempt, it is the self-protection of somebody who has already given up. And God said that sentence deliberately, in a place where she could hear it. Verse 10 says, "Sarah heard in the tent door, which was behind him" — he was saying it for her to hear.

The wounded heart says, "Why on earth should I be the one to pray for people as unjust as that?" You may have been hurt by someone, and that someone may now be in trouble himself. Brothers and sisters, I will not push you. I only want to point out one thing: in the city Abraham interceded for, there lived the nephew who had taken advantage of him. And from beginning to end the text never records Lot saying one word of thanks. We intercede not because the other person deserves it, but because our God is the God who says, "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked." And if you still cannot get the words out today, then pray first about your own wound — that is prayer too.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, say once more the thing you have stopped being able to laugh about. Find a quiet place and say to God, "Lord, I have stopped daring to ask for this." Then read verse 14 out loud: "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" Do not force yourself to feel certain. Only put it in front of him again.

Second, show hospitality to one person. This week invite somebody to a meal — preferably somebody you do not know well, or somebody you feel is of no use to you. Do a little more than you said you would, and then, while he is eating, stand at the side and pour him one more cup of water.

Third, add a "Sodom" to your prayer list. Think of one person you feel had it coming, one person you do not want to pray for, and pray for him three times this week. That one thing will change you more than it changes him.

Fourth, practise "going down to see." If you hear something negative about a person this week, then before you believe it or pass it on, stop and ask one question: have I checked this myself? Even God goes down to see.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. There is an eighty-nine-year-old woman in the Bible who heard God say that she would have a child the next year, and inside her tent she laughed to herself without making a sound. Then God said, "Why did Sarah laugh?" — he heard even the laugh that was only on the inside. And he did not withdraw the promise because of it; a year later the child was born, and his name means "he laughs."
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that he has heard every doubt inside me, and that he has not withdrawn his word because of it.
I declare that I will no longer use my own experience to limit what God is able to do.
I declare that although I am dust and ashes, I will still dare to speak to the Lord; I will intercede for the people I think had it coming.
I declare that at the very moment when I am most entitled to sit in the place of honour, I will choose to stand at the side and serve.
This week I am supposed to intercede for someone I dislike, but I cannot get the prayer out. What do I do?

Start at the lowest possible threshold. Step one: say only his name, and add one sentence — "Lord, you know." You do not have to ask anything for him, and you do not have to pretend you have forgiven him. Step two: do that three days running, and on the fourth day add one concrete blessing — ask God to give him peace, or to let him meet the right people. Step three: if hatred rises up inside you, say the hatred to God as well — Abraham was allowed to speak in God's presence. One thing to be careful about: interceding for him is not the same as agreeing that what he did was right, and it does not mean you have to go back into that relationship. All you are doing is moving him out of your courtroom and into God's.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sound from this lesson may remain, let it be the laugh that made no sound.
An eighty-nine-year-old woman, standing behind the curtain at the tent door, her back to the outside. She hears a stranger say: at about this time next year, you will have a son.
She laughed, once. No sound, nobody watching, not even her husband any the wiser. It is the kind of laugh that only comes from someone who has waited twenty-five years and has already shut the door.
And then a sentence comes in from outside: "Why did Sarah laugh?"
Brothers and sisters, in that moment she must have been terrified. And so she said: I didn't laugh.
And God said, "No, but you did laugh."
He did not let that denial pass — and he did not change a single thing because of it. Genesis 21:1: "Yahweh visited Sarah as he had said, and Yahweh did to Sarah as he had spoken."

And the child's name was Isaac — "he laughs". God wrote that bitter laugh into the name of the son of the promise. In 21:6, with the baby in her arms, Sarah said, "God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me."

One word, two kinds of laughter. One is a bitter laugh behind a closed door; the other is a great laugh with a child in her arms. Between them lie one year, and a God to whom the question is put: "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?"

The focus is not on whether I have believed enough, not on how long I have been unable to laugh, and not on how impossible the thing looks. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who hears the laugh inside me and still does exactly what he said he would do. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to hand over once more the thing we cannot laugh about, and to open our mouths in intercession for one person we think had it coming. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ A patriarch runs out to welcome three strangers. What correction does that picture make to the definition of "hospitality"?
2. ★★★ Why did God tell Abraham what he was about to do? What reason does the text itself give?
3. ★ Sarah laughed inside herself, and God did not shame her. What does the way God handled it let you see about him?
4. ★★ From fifty down to ten, the one who stopped was Abraham, not God. What reminder does that carry for your own intercession?

Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people "can say it", not that they "answer beautifully". If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I don't need to pray for people like that), fearful (what if I ask and it doesn't happen), ashamed (I am quietly laughing on the inside too), wounded (I once prayed for somebody and nothing ever came of it). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Is anything too hard for Yahweh?" Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ Is there something you say out loud that you believe, while on the inside you are quietly laughing at it? You do not have to say what it is. Only say this: when did that laugh first appear?
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The person I least want to pray for is …" If it is awkward to give a name, name the kind of person.
9. ★★ Who will you intercede for this week? Say how many days you will pray, and in which time slot.

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch the disappointment of prayers that were never answered. Do not explain God's reasons on his behalf, and never say "you did not ask hard enough." If someone brings up a relationship inside the group, deal with it privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ Hospitality that "says little and does much" — in your own home this week, who will you prepare a meal or a cup of water for?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who will you do a little extra for without saying anything about it?
12. ★★★ The intercession practice: this week, every day, say the name of one person you dislike and add the sentence "Lord, you know." Say which time slot you will do it in.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the person you are going to intercede for, and ask him to pray for him too. Say his name here and now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible who pleaded with God for a wicked city, going from fifty righteous men down to ten. Second, every single time God said yes, and the one who stopped first was the man. Third, so what I learned is this: when you plead for people, do not stop so early. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the person you will intercede for this week, and the person you will prepare that meal for. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to make our hearts towards people wider than our judgements about their affairs.
